rows.label: Concept
rows.text: The three elastic moduli — Young's (E), bulk (B), and shear (G) — quantify how materials resist stretching, uniform compression, and shape change respectively. Each is stress/strain with units N/m². They are related by E = 2G(1+σ) = 3B(1−2σ). Solids possess all three; fluids have only bulk modulus.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Young's modulus: E = (F/A)/(Δl/l) = Fl/(AΔl)
Bulk modulus: B = −P/(ΔV/V)
Shear modulus: G = (F/A)/θ = τ/θ

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Material State Determines Available Moduli:** Solids have all three moduli ($E, B, G$). Fluids (liquids/gases) have *only* bulk modulus $B$ — they cannot sustain shear stress ($G=0$) and have no defined Young's modulus for stretching.  ·  **Isotropic Material Relations:** For isotropic solids, the three moduli are linked via Poisson's ratio $\sigma$: $E = 2G(1+\sigma) = 3B(1-2\sigma)$. These relations *do not hold* for anisotropic materials (crystals, composites) where moduli depend on direction.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Choose the modulus by the type of deformation: stretch → E, squeeze → B, twist → G.  ·  The sign in B = −P/(ΔV/V) makes the modulus positive since ΔV is negative under compression.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Young: A 1 mm² wire, 2 m long, carrying 200 N extends 2 mm → E = (200/10⁻⁶)/(2×10⁻³/2) = 2×10¹¹ N/m².  ·  Bulk: 3×10⁶ Pa pressure shrinks 1 m³ of steel by 1.9×10⁻⁵ m³ → B = 1.6×10¹¹ Pa.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ 'All three moduli have different units.' ✅ All three are measured in N/m² (Pa) — same units, different deformation types.  ·  ❌ 'Bulk modulus applies only to liquids.' ✅ It applies to solids and gases too — any material under uniform pressure.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Compute Young's modulus from a wire experiment data set.  ·  Compute bulk modulus from a known pressure and volume change.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: unit memory: all three moduli are in N/m² (Pa).  ·  For Young's modulus: rearrange E = Fl/(AΔl) to solve any one variable.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: A 2 m copper wire of area 1 mm² extends by 1.2 mm under a 40 N load. Find Young's modulus for copper.  ·  Calculate the bulk modulus of a liquid if 2×10⁶ Pa pressure reduces 1.5 m³ of it by 0.75×10⁻³ m³.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: E, B, G definitions and units are certainty for short-answer questions.  ·  Young's modulus wire problems remain the most-tested numerical.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Young's modulus E = Fl/(AΔl) describes stretching/compression stiffness.  ·  Bulk modulus B = −P/(ΔV/V) describes compression under uniform pressure.  ·  Shear modulus G = τ/θ describes change of shape under tangential stress.  ·  The three moduli are interrelated: E = 2G(1+σ) = 3B(1−2σ).

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: E, B, G all have units N/m² (Pa) — they differ by the type of deformation they describe.  ·  E (stretching), B (volume), G (shape) measure the corresponding resistance of a material.  ·  The three moduli are linked: E = 2G(1+σ) and E = 3B(1−2σ).  ·  Liquids and gases have G = 0 (they cannot resist shear) — only solids have a shear modulus.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Thomas Young established the concept of the modulus of elasticity in 1807 — his modulus E is one of the most fundamental material constants.  ·  Rigidity (shear) modulus explains why liquids flow: their G = 0 — they cannot resist shear.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: A shear force of 5000 N acts on a 4 cm² face producing a shear angle of 0.01 rad. Find the shear modulus.  ·  Steel has E = 2×10¹¹ N/m² and G = 8×10¹⁰ N/m². Find Poisson's ratio from E = 2G(1+σ).  ·  A 10 m steel cable (E = 2×10¹¹) of area 2 cm² must not stretch more than 5 mm under load. Find the maximum load.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: The relation E = 2G(1+σ) is frequently used to find Poisson's ratio.  ·  Comparing bulk moduli of solids, liquids, gases comes up in conceptual questions.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Shear: A 2×10⁴ N force shears a 10⁻³ m² face by 2.5×10⁻³ rad → G = (2×10⁴/10⁻³)/2.5×10⁻³ = 8×10⁹ N/m².  ·  Relation check: E = 2G(1+σ) for steel: 2×10¹¹ = 2×8×10¹⁰(1+σ) → σ = 0.25.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: Young's modulus is the ratio of longitudinal stress to: → C  ·  A liquid has which elastic modulus? → C

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Young's modulus (E):** the ratio of longitudinal stress to longitudinal strain: E = (F/A)/(Δl/l) = Fl/(AΔl). It measures resistance to stretching/compression. For steel, E ≈ 2×10¹¹ N/m²; for aluminium ≈ 7×10¹⁰ N/m²; for rubber ≈ 5×10⁶ N/m².  ·  **Bulk modulus (B):** the ratio of volume stress (pressure) to volume strain: B = −P/(ΔV/V). It measures resistance to uniform compression. The minus sign keeps B positive (ΔV is negative under pressure). For water B ≈ 2.2×10⁹ Pa; steel B ≈ 1.6×10¹¹ Pa.  ·  **Shear modulus / modulus of rigidity (G or η):** the ratio of shear stress to shear strain: G = τ/θ = (F/A)/θ. It measures resistance to change of shape without change of volume. For steel G ≈ 8×10¹⁰ N/m².

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Fluids possess only bulk modulus; compressibility = 1/B.  ·  Relation: E = 2G(1 + σ) = 3B(1 − 2σ)  ·  Combined: E = 9BG/(3B + G); compressibility k = 1/B

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Geometry Separation:** $E$ is an intensive material property (Pa), while spring constant $k = EA/L$ is extensive. Changing a wire's length or cross-section changes $k$ but not $E$ — this distinction is essential for connecting spring problems to material science.  ·  Compressibility is the reciprocal of B.  ·  ❌ 'Shear strain is a length ratio.' ✅ Shear strain is the ANGLE of displacement θ (radians), not a length ratio.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ 'Young's modulus and stiffness k are the same.' ✅ Y and k connect through geometry: E = Fl/(AΔl) while k = F/Δl, so E = kL/A.  ·  ❌ 'Liquids have Young's modulus.' ✅ Liquids flow; they have NO shear modulus and no Young's modulus for stretching — only bulk modulus.  ·  ❌ 'B increases when you compress a solid.' ✅ B is a constant MATERIAL property within the elastic range; it does not change with the applied pressure.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Compressibility: water k = 1/B = 1/2.2×10⁹ = 4.5×10⁻¹⁰ Pa⁻¹.  ·  Convert areas to m² before computing stress (1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m², 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m²).  ·  The relation E = 2G(1+σ) lets you compute Poisson's ratio from E and G.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: NEB commonly asks to compute one modulus from two others using the linking relations.  ·  Each modulus = stress/strain: E (longitudinal), B (volume), G (shear) — pick by the deformation type.  ·  E, B and G are linked by Poisson's ratio σ: E = 2G(1+σ) = 3B(1−2σ).
